prs.title: export: only send each static generation batch its own resume data cache seeds
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

During the final static generation phase (fallback shells with Cache Components), each export worker batch now receives only the resume data cache (RDC) seeds for its own pages. It no longer receives the seed map for the whole build.

### Why?

`exportPagesInBatches` sent the complete `renderResumeDataCachesByPage` map to every batch. Each seed is a serialized resume data cache, so with large `'use cache'` values and many fallback shells this message grows with the whole build rather than with the batch. Messages to child-process workers are JSON-encoded into a single string. Once that string exceeds V8's maximum string length (about 512 MiB), `next build` fails with a bare `RangeError: Invalid string length`. That happens in both child-process and `experimental.workerThreads` mode. This is one of the two failure directions behind #99850.

Example: 12 locales under `/[lang]/[slug]` (13 fallback shells), with about 40 MiB of cached data per shell and `staticGenerationMinPagesPerWorker: 1`. Every batch received a seed map of about 686M characters and the build failed, even though no single batch needed more than a fraction of it.

### How?

- **Filtering:** an inline loop in `exportPagesInBatches` picks out the seeds whose page key matches a path in the batch. The initial phase, which has no seed map, is unchanged. How seeds are chosen (`buildRDCCacheByPage`) is unchanged.
- **Shared page key:** the `page: path` key that seeds are stored and looked up under is now a 
…(truncated)

prs.title: turbo-tasks: update reader leaf distance inline when adding output dependency
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### What?

Updates the reader's leaf distance inline when `try_read_task_output` adds a new output-dependency edge. The `LeafDistanceUpdateQueue` is only used to propagate to the reader's existing output dependents.

### Why?

The reader is already locked (with the `All` category) while the edge is added. Before this change, the code allocated a fresh `LeafDistanceUpdateQueue` and pushed the reader into it. After dropping the guards it locked the reader again, just to update one field.

In the common case the reader has no output dependents yet, so all of that work was redundant. This path runs for each new edge whose reader's distance is not already greater than the dependency's, which is common in cold builds with dependency tracking enabled.

### How?

- The leaf-distance arithmetic now lives in a single `compute_leaf_distance_update`, used by both the queue and the inline path. The arithmetic itself is unchanged.
- At the call site:
  - The new distance is written on the reader guard that is already held.
  - Output-dependent IDs are snapshotted into a `SmallVec`.
  - The paired-lock dependency registration is unchanged.
  - The queue is only created, seeded and executed after both guards are dropped.
- The `trace_leaf_distance_update` tracing stays supported via an inline span.

### Verification

- New behavioral unit tests for how leaf distance propagates:
  - a reader that is already ahead of its dependency is not updated;
  - a reader at or behind its dependency moves
…(truncated)

prs.title: bench: add warm cached build benchmark to nested-deps-app-router-many-pages
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds `bench-warm-build.mjs` (plus a `bench-warm-build` script entry) to `bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages`. It benchmarks warm Turbopack compiles of `next build` with the persistent filesystem cache, after changing N source files.

```bash
cd bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages
pnpm prepare-bench
node bench-warm-build.mjs --files=1000
```

### Why?

To measure the incremental rebuild work of a cached build after many changes on a large app, e.g. for turbo-tasks scheduler changes like #100561. Until now there was no easy way to do that.

### How?

- **Cold compile:** an optional cold compile (deletes `.next`) fills the cache. It is reported but not counted.
- **Warm compiles:** by default, 20 warm compiles run (`--iterations=20`). The first 5 are warm-up (`--warmup=5`): they are printed but excluded from the statistics.
  - Each warm iteration changes N component files from `components/`, picked deterministically with a seeded shuffle.
  - The change is a rendered JSX attribute with a per-run/per-iteration value (digits only), so it changes the emitted code (not just a comment) and always differs from what is cached. A file that is still changed from an earlier, killed run is changed again rather than failing.
- **Statistics:** wall time and the "Compiled successfully in" time are printed per iteration. Over the non-warm-up builds, the script prints count, median, mean, sample standard deviation, min and max.
- **Compile only:** builds use `--experimental

prs.title: turbopack: merge chunk group lists in parallel in compute_merged_modules
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Merges the per-chunk `lists_reverse_indices` and `intra_group_references_rev` maps of `compute_merged_modules` in parallel, instead of entry by entry on one thread.

This is the second of three stacked PRs; it is based on #100236.
1. intern bitmaps (#100236)
2. parallel merge of the chunk group lists (this PR)
3. reconciliation shortcuts (#100238)

### Why?

After `map chunk groups`, the per-chunk results were folded into one map with `entry(key).or_default().extend(set)` on a single thread. On the bench app below that is ~19.1 M list occurrences, merged in a 1.7 s step on one core.

### How?

New private helper `merge_index_maps_of_sets(parts, shard_count)`:
- **Split:** in parallel, each part is split into shards by the high bits of the key's FxHash (`(hash as u128 * shard_count as u128) >> 64`). Each key's position (part index, index in part) is recorded.
- **Merge:** in parallel, each shard merges its buckets in part order. The first set of a key is moved instead of copied, and later sets extend it.
- **Order:** the shard results are concatenated and stably sorted by each key's first position. Each shard's output is already sorted by position, so the stable sort merges those runs. Positions are unique, so stability doesn't change the result.
- **One shard:** when `shard_count` is 0 or 1, the parts are merged serially into the first part instead: it reserves the remaining parts' lengths, moves sets for new keys and extends existing ones. No bucketing, regrouping
…(truncated)

prs.title: perf(build): avoid O(pages²) original app path scan in static check
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Removes a quadratic scan from the `static-check` phase of `next build`. The original app paths for each App Router page are now looked up from an index that is built once, instead of being rediscovered by scanning every route for every page.

### Why?

Inside the per-page `check-page` work, each app page walked all of `appPathRoutes` (allocating a fresh entries array each time) to find the original app paths that normalize to it. That is O(pages²), and it runs synchronously on the main thread before `isPageStatic` is dispatched, so build workers sit idle while it runs. On apps with thousands of routes this was a significant share of `static-check`.

### How?

Before the pages are fanned out, the build makes one pass over `appPathRoutes` and groups original app paths by their normalized pathname. It applies the same `mappedAppPages` filter the old per-page loop used, and preserves the same per-group order. Each page then does a single lookup and hands the result to the existing `selectAppPageEntry`, which picks the winning entry exactly as before. Pages with no matching entry keep the previous behavior. Pages Router handling is unchanged.

Cost goes from O(pages × routes) to O(routes) plus one map lookup per page.

### Verification

`bench/nested-deps-app-router-many-pages` (3,000 generated pages, Turbopack, 8 cores). Compiled once, then ran `next build --experimental-build-mode=generate` 3× before and 3× after the change, each from the same compiled output:

| | Ru

prs.title: Turbopack: ensure tests are dropping turbo tasks correctly
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Let the unit tests check if we cleanup correctly: after `stop_and_wait()`, the test harness checks that it holds the only reference to the `TurboTasks` instance, then drops it.

Recreates #85612, rebased on latest `canary`.

### Details

- `stop_and_wait()` returns once all jobs have signaled completion, but the spawned futures that ran them (e.g. priority-runner workers, background jobs) may still be dropping their `Arc<TurboTasks>` clones at that point. An immediate `Arc::strong_count == 1` assertion therefore fails nondeterministically (33 of 1166 tests locally), even though the references are released shortly after.
- Instead of adding tracking overhead to the manager, the harness polls (1 ms sleeps) until `Arc::strong_count` reaches 1, and panics with the remaining reference count after 10 s. Real leaks are still caught.
- Adapted to `TestInstance`: the `snapshot_and_evict` closure (which holds its own reference) is dropped before the check.

### Verification

- `cargo nextest run` for turbo-tasks-backend, turbo-tasks-fetch, turbo-tasks-fs, turbo-tasks-macros-tests, turbopack-analyze, turbopack-core, turbopack-ecmascript, turbopack-node, turbo-tasks-testing: 1166 passed.
- turbo-tasks-backend + turbo-tasks-fetch repeated 3×: all passing.

prs.title: Turbopack: add minServerChunkSize and maxMergeServerChunkSize options
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Adds two experimental options under `experimental.turbopackChunking`:

- `minServerChunkSize` — the minimum chunk size used by Turbopack's production chunker for Node.js server-side JavaScript.
- `maxMergeServerChunkSize` — the size above which a Node.js server chunk is never merged with other chunks.

Both apply only to the Node.js server chunking context (production builds only). Edge chunking is unchanged and not configurable.

### Why?

`minChunkSize` / `maxMergeChunkSize` only affect client-side chunking. The Node.js server context used hardcoded thresholds, so there was no way to tune server chunking (e.g. to trade fewer, larger server chunks against duplication).

Edge is intentionally left out: Edge functions have a much smaller size limit, so its existing hardcoded thresholds (min `20000`, no max merge limit) are kept as-is.

### How?

- The options follow the same path as the existing client thresholds: config type + zod schema → `TurbopackChunkingConfig` / `TurbopackChunking` in `next-core` → `Project` → `ServerChunkingContextOptions`, used by both the regular and the `_with_client_assets` Node.js variants.
- When unset, the previously hardcoded Node.js values are used (min `4000`, max merge `100000`), so default output is unchanged.
- Only the ECMAScript chunk type is affected; client chunking, CSS chunking and the edge chunking context are untouched.
- Docs: new "Server Chunks" section in the `turbopackChunking` reference (noting that Edge isn't affect

prs.title: Render complete HTML documents after MPA Server Actions
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
MPA form submissions to Cache Components pages could return only the continuation of a prerender. The action executed, but the response omitted the HTML document and did not render the returned `useActionState` value.

This change renders a complete document for MPA form submissions while retaining the RDC supplied by the prerender. This preserves ordinary `'use cache'` values on deployments where the default handler has no prerendered entries in memory. The action handler also prepares the render phase for MPA form submissions that do not revalidate data. Ordinary not-found responses include the root layout.

The diagnosis and reproduction in #99981 identified the self-hosted case. This fix also handles postponed state supplied by Vercel before the action body, without changing how that body is decoded.

The tests cover plain and stateful forms, both postponed-state variants, submission before hydration, cache reuse, invalidation, blocking routes, and ordinary and global not-found responses.

Fixes #99756
Closes #99981

prs.title: Optimize persistence CPU
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
A few small optimizations from profiling

* Replace SmallVec with Vec for our encoding buffer
    - During persistence these are pooled and preallocated so we never benefit from the inline storage
    - SmallVec places branches around core operations which complicate codegen
* Avoid temporary allocations during encoding via a new 'filtered collection encode primitive'.  This allows us to guess a size and fix it later by overwriting the varint.
* Expand the SST Writer output buffer to 256K to reduce the number of `write` syscalls by about 90%
* Update to the new bincode-fork location in vercel-labs, which also picks up a small varint encoding win

Altogether these saved about 10% cpu time and 25% wall time for v0 persistence

prs.author: sokra

### What?

Two changes to the reverse postorder ranks that the RPO stack computes before each fixed-point traversal:

prs.title: Stamp FileSystemCache revalidations and entries with the monotonic clock
prs.author: skrabe
prs.body:
### What?
`FileSystemCache` dates tag revalidations and cache entries with the wall clock, but since #94457 `areTagsExpired` compares them against the monotonic clock (`performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`).
When the wall clock runs ahead, a revalidation is dated in the future, so it's ignored and the old page keeps being served.

### Why?
I ran into this with `next start`, when our E2E tests kept getting stale pages after `revalidateTag`. In a fresh 16.4.2 app with the wall clock 5ms ahead, 30 out of 30 reads right after a revalidation returned the old page. With this change, it's 0 of 30.

The two clocks drift apart in ordinary setups, for example when NTP, a VM or WSL2 corrects the wall clock while the server runs.

### How?
Use the monotonic clock everywhere that `FileSystemCache` dates something, as `incremental-cache/index.ts` already does:

- `revalidateTag` and `set()` stamp with `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()` instead of `Date.now()`.
- `set()` also stores that timestamp on disk, as `routeCacheLastModified` in the `.meta` file and as `lastModified` in the fetch cache entry. Reads used to take the file's mtime(wall-clock time).
  Files without a stored time, from `next build` or an older Next.js version, still fall back to the mtime. They were written before the server started, so their mtime is earlier than any revalidation it records.
This matters when entries are read from disk: with `cacheMaxMemorySize: 0`, or after an eviction from the memory 
…(truncated)

prs.title: Turbopack: compute client reference manifest parts once per reference, not per page
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

When Turbopack builds an app's client reference manifests, it builds one per app entry (page). For each client reference a page uses, `build_manifest` recomputed:

- the reference's server path;
- its client, SSR and RSC module ids (each read goes through the chunking context's id strategy, the module's ident and a keyed module-id map read);
- for every JS chunk, its component chunks (the merged chunk's runtime info plus each component chunk's path and file size).

None of these depend on the page, and pages usually share most of their client references. So the number of reads grew as pages × references, and with `experimental.turbopackChunking.generateComponentChunks` as pages × references × chunks × component chunks. Every read was also another dependency edge on each page's `build_manifest` task.

This PR moves that work into two turbo-tasks functions that are keyed only on page-independent inputs:

- `client_reference_ids`: keyed on the client reference module, the client chunking context and the optional SSR chunking context. It returns the server path and the client, SSR and RSC module ids.
- `client_chunk_components`: keyed on the chunk and the client-relative path. It returns the chunk's component chunk paths and sizes.

Each page's manifest now does one cached read per reference and one per chunk. Values and insertion order are unchanged, so the generated manifests are the same. After an edit, only the tasks whose inputs changed rerun.

prs.title: Persist storage cache in Docker environments
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Next.js now persists its server-side storage cache in Docker environments, the same as other environments. This covers the RSC / Server Actions encryption key, preview-mode keys, and the development Chrome DevTools workspace identifier.

### Why?

The shared storage-directory helper previously disabled `.next/cache` persistence whenever Docker was detected. As a result, Docker environments could not reuse cached RSC encryption secrets across separate key-generation processes.

### How?

The shared helper now always resolves the cache directory beneath the configured dist directory. Because storage is always available, each consumer drops the now-unreachable fallback path and uses the existing cache read/write flow directly. Existing key validation, expiry-based rotation during builds, and `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` precedence are unchanged.

Telemetry is intentionally unchanged: it has its own storage-location logic for CI and Docker, which already stores telemetry configuration in `.next/cache` there.

### Verification

- Ran a focused probe against the updated source with Docker detection mocked. It confirmed RSC encryption-key cache write and reuse, expired-key handling for runtime and builds, explicit encryption-key precedence, and preview-key cache write and reuse.
- `pnpm --filter=next types`
- Not run: full Next.js integration tests.

prs.title: turbo-tasks-backend: resolve task priority when creating child contexts
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

`ExecuteContext::child_context()` in `turbo-tasks-backend` now reads the current task priority on the calling thread. The resulting `ChildExecuteContext` stores a priority that is already known, instead of an optional one.

### Why?

Both users of `child_context()` hand the child context to `scope_bounded` helper threads:

- the parallel path of `connect_children` (≥10k new children)
- the parallel invalidation of output dependents

Before this change the child context copied an override that is usually unset. On a helper thread, `get_current_task_priority()` then fell back to the task-local task state. That state only exists on the thread running the task, so helper threads got `TaskPriority::initial()`. Tasks scheduled or made dirty from those chunks (e.g. via `make_task_dirty_internal`) therefore got a priority that depended on which thread ran the chunk.

### How?

The priority is resolved in `child_context()`, on the thread that creates the context. An explicit override still wins; otherwise the task-local priority is read before the work moves to another thread. Making the field non-optional means a child context can no longer carry an unresolved priority.

Putting the fix in `child_context()` covers both parallel users, and any future one. Neither user relied on the late lookup, because the child context always runs on another thread. Paths that don't go parallel are unchanged.

- `cargo check -p turbo-tasks-backend --all-targets`
- `cargo cli

## Summary

Proposes repository-level worktree setup for Codex and Claude Code, replacing the worktree instructions in AGENTS.md. A shared script installs dependencies and builds Next.js with its workspace dependencies. Codex runs it through a local environment; Claude creates a detached HEAD worktree and runs the same setup.

Claude cleanup preserves uncommitted changes and commits that are not reachable from a branch or tag. Codex's environment must be selected when starting a worktree chat.

prs.title: [testmode] Fix compressed HTTP responses with test proxy
prs.author: kassens
prs.body:
## Summary

Fix compressed responses received by Node HTTP clients when `experimental.testProxy` is enabled. Requests outside a test context and proxy `continue` responses now use native HTTP passthrough, preserving the original compressed bytes and headers.

Normalize stale `Content-Encoding` and `Content-Length` headers when serializing fetched responses with supported compression encodings, including cloned fetch responses. Preserve explicitly constructed mock responses as supplied, including deliberately compressed bytes. Handlers that construct a response with a modified body must update its headers themselves. Preserve bodyless responses such as HEAD so their representation metadata remains available.

Add regression coverage for chunked responses and compressed bodies whose decoded length is shorter or longer than the upstream content length, across native passthrough, proxy continue, fetched responses, and modified responses. Also cover explicitly compressed mocks, fetched-response clones, unsupported encodings, and HEAD metadata.

## Verification

- All 36 testmode integration tests passed in development mode with webpack, using the published native binding because the local native build has an incompatible lockfile API.
- Confirmed the standalone gzip reproduction fails against the unchanged build and passes with native passthrough.

prs.title: Use fixed encoding for our 'id' types
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
Varint encoding works well for things like lengths/indicies which are naturally 'zero biased' but many of our 'id' types are not like that

Switch them to use a fixed encoding

This includes:

* `TaskId` mostly 5 bytes before, now 4 bytes always
* `CellId` always 5 bytes before, now 4 bytes always
* `RawVc` always 9 bytes before, 8 bytes now
* `FunctionId` mostly 3 bytes before, now 2 bytes
* `ValueTypeId` mostly 3 bytes before now 2 bytes
* `TraitTypeId` transformed to a `NonZeroU8` so it always takes the fixed int encode path naturally

In principle it is possible that we might still benefit from varint encoding if most of the uses of these ids were biased towards smaller values, but at least in practice this isn't the case.

### Results

Measured on a large app comparing to canary

| | canary | this PR | change | per-round range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cache size after cold build** | 2.646 GB | 2.546 GB | **−3.8%** | −3.8 to −3.7% |
| **Cache size after warm build** (compacted) | 2.628 GB | 2.527 GB | **−3.8%** | −3.9 to −3.7% |
| **Warm build user CPU** (mostly decoding) | 43.8s | 42.2s | **−3.7%** | −5.1 to −2.3% |
| Cold build user CPU | 482.6s | 483.0s | +0.1% | −1.4 to +1.0% |
| Wall time, cold / warm | 75.3s / 31.2s | 76.1s / 31.4s | within noise | |
| Peak RSS, cold / warm | | | −0.2% / −0.8% | |

### What?

This PR adds a new example, `examples/eve`. The example runs an [eve](https://eve.dev) agent and a Next.js App Router app as one project. It uses the `eve/next` integration.

### Why?

Next.js does not have an example that shows how to add an eve agent to an app. This example gives a minimal starting point.

You can create the example with `create-next-app --example eve`. You can deploy it with the Deploy button. The agent and the app use the same origin. They deploy as one Vercel project.

prs.title: Create cache directory before persisting Chrome DevTools workspace UUID
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

When the dev server answers the Chrome DevTools workspace request (`/.well-known/appspecific/com.chrome.devtools.json`) and there's no persisted UUID yet, it now creates `<distDir>/cache` before writing `chrome-devtools-workspace-uuid`.

### Why?

The UUID was written with a bare `writeFile`. If the cache directory didn't exist at the time of the first DevTools request (e.g. it was removed while `next dev` was running), the write failed with `ENOENT`. That logged the "needs to be reconnected after the next page reload" warning and kept the UUID in memory only, so the next server process generated a new UUID and the DevTools workspace had to be reconnected.

On a normal startup the directory usually already exists because other startup writers create it, which is why this rarely shows up.

### How?

- The directory is created recursively inside the existing `try/catch`. If creating the directory or writing the file fails (e.g. an unwritable path), the endpoint still responds with an in-memory UUID and logs the existing warning.

**Test:** a dev-only e2e test (`// @force-gate dev`) in `test/e2e/chrome-devtools-workspace/`, using a dedicated fixture:
- It waits for the asynchronous startup writes into the cache directory (`.rscinfo`, plus `next-devtools-config.json` with webpack), then removes the directory.
- It then checks the endpoint returns a UUID, that the same UUID is on disk, and that no persistence warning is logged. After restarting the server, the same UUID

prs.title: turbo-bitset: make block storage pluggable
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

`turbo_bitset::Bitset` can now use different storage for its blocks. A new public `BlockStorage` trait defines what that storage must support.

- `Bitset` is now `Bitset<S: BlockStorage = Vec<usize>>`, so every existing user keeps `Vec<usize>` storage.
- The trait is implemented for `Vec<usize>`, `SmallVec<[usize; N]>` and `ArrayVec<usize, N>`. `turbo-bitset` now depends on `smallvec` and `arrayvec` unconditionally.
- All `Bitset` methods and operators, plus `Encode`, `Decode` and `ShrinkToFit`, work with any storage. Set operations require both sides to use the same storage. The `turbo-tasks` integrations remain on the default `Bitset`.
- The encoding doesn't depend on the storage, so bytes written with one storage decode into any other.
- With `ArrayVec`, operations that would need more than its capacity of `N` blocks panic. Decoding a set that doesn't fit returns a `DecodeError`.
- `shrink_to_fit` only touches the storage when that frees capacity. An `ArrayVec` or an inline `SmallVec` is left unchanged.

### Why?

This lets small sets use inline storage where that helps, without making every `Bitset` user change its storage type.

### How?

- **Bounded storage:** when an operation would exceed an `ArrayVec`'s capacity, empty blocks at either end of the storage are dropped first. This fixes a case where an insert at the back panicked although the bits fit, because earlier growth at the front had filled the capacity with zero blocks.

prs.title: Add a CLI for reviewing agent feedback
prs.author: aurorascharff
prs.body:
## Why

Agent Feedback reports are created inside coding environments that often cannot launch a local browser. The previous instructions made the final handoff depend on the agent finding and invoking host-specific browser tooling. In headless, sandboxed, or remote sessions, that step could fail even when the anonymized report itself was valid, leaving the maintainer without a usable review link.

This happened in practice when an agent could not share its feedback and had to be told to run a browser command manually. Browser control should not be part of the Agent Feedback reporting contract.

## What changed

- add the hidden `next internal agent-feedback [report]` command as the supported handoff for an encoded v5 Agent Feedback report
- keep the command internal because it is protocol machinery, not a public semver-covered CLI surface
- accept the report as a positional argument or through stdin, validate the complete v5 schema, and always print the review URL before attempting to open the default browser
- preserve the printed URL when browser launching is unavailable or fails
- bound stdin to 16 KiB and a five-second read deadline using Node's async iterator and `AbortController`
- support `--dry-run` for validation and URL generation without opening a browser
- update the Agent Feedback protocol and evals to use the internal CLI instead of host-specific browser commands

This keeps the report anonymized and makes CLI output—not browser availability—the reliable source
